title: Apply innovative thinking to the development of a small business

lessons.title: What innovation means for a small agri-business
lessons.html:
Innovation is not only inventions

Innovation means finding a new or better way to create value for customers. In a small business it is seldom a new machine or a patent. More often it is a new product, a better process, a new market or a smarter way of working. For a small farming or packhouse business, examples include:

  • New product: turning class 2 fruit that cannot be exported into dried fruit, juice or jam for the local market.
  • New process: using a simple app or spreadsheet to track bins and pickers, saving hours of paperwork.
  • New market: selling directly to restaurants, school feeding schemes or a farm stall instead of only to a fresh produce market.
  • New service: offering cold storage space or packing services to neighbouring small growers.
  • New business model: subscription boxes of seasonal fruit delivered to homes in town.

Creative thinking techniques

Innovative ideas come more easily when you use deliberate techniques:

  • Brainstorming: a group writes down as many ideas as possible without judging them, then sorts them later.
  • Asking why and what if: why do we always sell to the same agent? What if we packed in smaller punnets?
  • Looking at problems as opportunities: fruit wasted because of hail marks could become a product for processors.
  • Learning from other industries: how do online shops deliver, and could we do the same with vegetables?
  • Listening to customers: complaints and requests point to unmet needs.
  • Mind maps: draw the main problem in the centre and branch out with causes, ideas and links.

Barriers to innovation

People often resist change because of fear of failure, lack of money or time, or the belief that the way things have always been done is the only way. A small business owner can reduce these barriers by testing ideas on a small scale, involving workers in finding solutions and rewarding good suggestions.

lessons.title: Evaluating and implementing innovative ideas
lessons.html:
From idea to opportunity

Not every idea is a good business opportunity. Before spending money, evaluate each idea against simple questions:

  1. Is there a real customer need? Who will buy it, and why would they choose it over what they buy now?
  2. Can we do it? Do we have the skills, equipment, land, water and people, or can we get them?
  3. Will it make money? Estimate the selling price, the cost per unit and the number you can sell.
  4. What are the risks? Weather, competition, regulations such as food safety rules, and reliance on one buyer.
  5. Does it fit our business? Does it support what we already do, or distract from it?

A simple scoring table, where each idea gets a score of 1 to 5 on each question, helps compare ideas fairly.

Testing on a small scale

Before investing heavily, run a pilot. For example, a small grower thinking of selling fruit boxes in town can start with 20 boxes a week to friends and colleagues, record costs and feedback, and adjust the price and contents. Only when the pilot shows demand and profit should the business invest in a delivery vehicle or cold room.

Implementing the idea

  • Write a short action plan: what will be done, by whom, by when and with what budget.
  • Check legal requirements, such as food safety rules for processed products, labelling, business registration and tax.
  • Communicate the change to workers and train them.
  • Monitor results against targets each week or month.
  • Improve the idea based on what you learn.

Protecting your idea

Some ideas, such as a brand name or logo, can be protected by registering a trade mark. Simpler protection includes keeping recipes or methods confidential and building strong relationships with customers.

Key points

  • Innovation can be a new product, process, market, service or business model.
  • Use techniques like brainstorming, what-if questions and customer feedback.
  • Evaluate ideas for need, capability, profit, risk and fit.
  • Test ideas with a small pilot before investing heavily.
  • Implement with an action plan, training and monitoring.
